title: Why a Curve Symmetric About the x-Axis Cannot Be a Non-Zero Function
originalTopic: Theory and Examples: Symmetry and Function Definition
author: Muhammad Abdullah Athar
problemStatement: A curve in the xy-plane is symmetric about the x-axis if and only if whenever (x, y) lies on the curve, (x, -y) also lies on the curve. Explain why a curve that is symmetric about the x-axis cannot be the graph of a function of x, unless the function is identically y = 0.
finalAnswer: \text{Any point } (x_0, y_0) \text{ with } y_0 \ne 0 \text{ yields two distinct outputs } y_0 \text{ and } -y_0 \text{ for } x_0

steps.title: Suppose the Curve Contains a Point with y_0 != 0
steps.explanation: Assume a curve symmetric about the x-axis contains at least one point (x_0, y_0) where y_0 != 0. By definition of x-axis symmetry, the reflected point (x_0, -y_0) must also lie on the curve.
steps.why: Symmetry across the x-axis pairs every point (x, y) on the curve with (x, -y).

steps.title: Show That the Uniqueness Condition of a Function Is Violated
steps.explanation: Because y_0 != 0, the numbers y_0 and -y_0 are distinct. Thus the single input x_0 corresponds to two distinct outputs y_0 and -y_0, meaning the vertical line x = x_0 intersects the curve at least twice.
steps.why: A real number equals its own negation (y = -y) if and only if y = 0.

steps.title: Conclude the Exception y = 0
steps.explanation: Consequently, for a curve symmetric about the x-axis to pass the Vertical Line Test, every point (x, y) on the curve must satisfy y = -y, which forces y = 0 for all x in the domain.
steps.why: Only points lying directly on the x-axis (y = 0) remain fixed under reflection across the x-axis.
